string.text: I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Shall I tell you my story?
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.

From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Now, in Urkhun's day, if a akan apprenticed in siegecraft went to work for another master, it meant a very painful death if he was recaptured. But times have changed. The richest plums of the empire's cities have fallen, and they build their walls higher than they once did. The akan lords pay less for a siegemaster, and that pay is often late. So I am up to taking other employment, if it is offered.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Of course, of course. A good engineer deserves his pay.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. How virtue has crumbled since the old days.

I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Indeed... Well, at any rate, if you find there is an inconvenient wall between you and the object of your desire, and you wish it reduced to rubble, you know where to find me.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. You know, you'd think this place could serve proper kumis, instead of this piss they call wine... Sorry, where were we? Ah yes, my story.
I marched with the Asafo companies, bearing shield and spear for my chief.

I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. So I went to her brother, and offered him 50 sheep - a good price. But he said he wasn't giving his sister to a 'man like me.' Asked him what he meant by that, and he didn't answer, so I gave him a good punch. Maybe a couple punches - no more. Shouldn't have hurt a real man, but this little whelp died on me.

I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Well, you know how these things go - his kin came to our village looking for my blood. They didn't find me, but wounded one of my cousins. It was time to teach them a lesson, but my brothers had a fit of cowardice. So they brokered a deal, and I was forced to leave. How do you like that?
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. Aye, real honor is as scarce as hen's teeth these days.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Strange thing, how people don't wish to die in someone else's quarrel.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Let me tell you something - I'm sick of cowardice, sick of those who don't stand by their comrades and their kin.
I marched with the Asafo companies, bearing shield and spear for my chief.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.

I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. MY family said others would mock my father's memory. They said no one would fear to steal our sheep and horses, to molest my sisters. They told me I had a choice: do my duty, or I would no longer be of their blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die?
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. A noble decision!
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. What? Does no one respect their parents anymore?

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. If an enemy chooses to stand in a battle-line and face my arrows, I would not hesitate to kill him. But our feuds - I cannot accept that I have no choice but to kill a man who had no choice but to be my enemy. I left my people. Here I can choose what I do.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Yeah... I'll tell you a tale of life in the great akan hordes, terror of the world.

I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. I've fought for Ulus Khan, and for Monchug Khan, and even for the old Urkhun. But I fight on foot - my family's from the town, not the steppe. Life's a little different for us.

I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. The horse lords, the men of the great tribes - well they gallop here, and they gallup there, shooting this and shooting that. They win battles, I'll give them that. But at the end of the day, if the enemy's still laughing at you behind their walls, all that galloping means nothing.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. We foot-sloggers, we're the ones who go up the ladder and into the meat grinder. Did that for 15 years, and I'm still getting less pay than some boy fresh of his mother's tit who happens to own a horse. Piss on that, I said, and I went looking for other work.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Indeed. Good infantry is the backbone of an army.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Resentment is poison to an army. Men must learn to follow what orders they are given.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. At any rate, I'll fight for any man willing to take the same risks that his men face.
I marched with the Asafo companies, bearing shield and spear for my chief.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. I'll tell you my story. But if you would judge me for what I do, you're welcome to do so, but I do not care to hear it.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.

I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. They protected us, but they treated us with contempt. We were told to hew wood for them, to bring them water. We submitted. For the sake of our old, of our nursing mothers, we submitted. But it was hard for the young men to take.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Indeed. Misfortune does not mean you must submit to humiliation.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. As well they should have. Those who curse their protectors deserve no home.
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Ah... Very well, I can satisfy your curiosity.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. If a man was drunk enough, I could usually take their purse without them even knowing, although sometimes they required a small knock on the head. Only travellers, though - much less fuss afterwards. Every trade takes finesse, as my father said.

From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. A wise man, my father. But proud, and that was his undoing. A thief cannot be proud. We do not survive long without protection from the guards, and a new captain wanted to double the 'tax' my father paid. He refused, so they hanged him.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. I guess there's something to be learned from those skilled at all trades.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Sounds like justice served.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. I too am proud. So, I cannot work as a thief. Now I am looking for work that doesn't require me to bend down to the whims of guards, dogs and turnkeys.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Shall I tell you my story?
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.
My clan lived by the stool of our chief, but I was cast out for choosing a different path.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. Such a cruel decree...
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Sensible man, that Urkhun. Nomads are the enemy of order.

I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. I have scraped together a few coins. I will not say how, but they were enough to buy a sword. I am determined to earn enough to buy my people what was taken away from them - herds. I am sad to say I know little of the steppe, but I know much of the towns, of the back streets, of how to live in the gutters and shadows and grow strong.

I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Urkhun Khan decreed a generation ago that all the akans must settle, to be conscripted and taxed. We refused. His men took our flocks, and we have since lived like beggars on the edge of the towns. I have resolved to go out and earn the money we need to buy new flocks, and then we shall go again into the great grass, beyond the reach of any tyrant or khan.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Oh yes. I do indeed have a story to tell you.
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. I feel no guilt - they were trying to kill me, and some came very close. I did what I needed to do.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Yes, I suppose you did what you had to do.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Necessity or not, you seem to take pride in what you did.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. There's not much more to say. My master was a sadistic animal but he let me keep my winnings, and eventually buy my freedom. I think he may also have realized that eventually, had he kept me against my will, he'd have ended up with a severed neck vein. So here I am, looking to make a living through the only means I know - shedding other people's blood. Got work?
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Well, if you wish to know how cruel a pack can be to one of its own, I could enlighten you.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. I wandered a bit on the steppe. I starved a bit. But I followed the raiders and one, when he went beyond the campfire to empty his bladder, did not return. I now have his purse and his sword.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. I'm sorry for your loss. You drew a cruel lot in life.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Every day, I give thanks to the Heavens that I was not born a savage.

I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. I could return to my people, I suppose, but I have no wish to do so. So I am here, in the towns, where I can make good money with my sword and care nothing about those who envy me.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. Shall I tell you my story?
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.
I was taken by slavers once, but I bought back my freedom with blood and sweat.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. I'm sure he'll be happy if you're happy.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. You must have broken your poor father's heart.
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Mm. Oh yes, you may.
My father was a craftsman of the Akan people. He taught me goldwork, farming, and the pride of our clan.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. At any rate, that wasn't the life for me. So I made up my mind to run off to the grasses, find one of those tribes that doesn't answer to the khan and takes in fugitives. The Karaakans, they call them. Problem is I first needed a horse.

From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Anyway I hung around the marketplace in Chaikand, looking for a likely candidate. Eventually I found an animal whose owner hadn't tied up too well as he went off to get drunk. So I took it and ran. And you know what? The cursed beast threw me, not one league out of town, and ran back to his sodden master.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Oh well. I guess you've got spirit.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Hah! May all thieves fail as you did.
I grew up among traders, learning the ways of gold dust, kola, and cloth.

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. I was the son of a village peddler but that's not the kind of life I want to live. I want to learn to fight and ride. There are a lot of us lads like that in the akan lands, I think you'll find, even if the great horse lords think we're fit only to stitch sandals or push a plough.

Hmm. Many men would begin their story by reciting their ancestry. I will not do this. A man should be judged on his own deeds, and a long list of ancestors does him no credit. Also, my family does not acknowledge me, so why should I acknowledge them?

I was the son of a slave. My master, a judge, raised me in his house, but it was clear that he would never spend much time to ensure my success in the world. Still, I was tutored with his other sons, and chose to study medicine as a young man. I thought I could perhaps be a physician.

Well... I was soon disabused of this idea. A doctor starting out in the world must either have a great deal of money, or family that ensures him a long list of clients. I had neither. Instead of working in the city, I took service aboard a ship.

Professionally, it was perhaps the best thing I could have done. Fevers, injuries, festering sores - the seaman has in greater number and variety than any manner of land-dweller, I imagine. But I have little patience for life aboard, the monotony, the tyranny of captains, the lack of any space to oneself, the groaning of timbers, the constant smell of rotting bilge...
Yes, it must be trying.
Weren't handed life on a silver platter, were you? Such a tragedy.
At any rate, I have a bit of money to my name, and the leisure to wait a few weeks before choosing my next employer.

I was the son of a slave, but my father bought me my freedom and an apprenticeship with a healer. I could make a lot of money as a doctor if I came from a well-known family that would attract patients. But I don't, so I offer my skills to war-leaders, who cannot afford to be so picky.
I shall tell you... Ahem...

My father is Aytham, son of Thamuq, who was son of Munbilas - the elder son, mind you, not the younger - and he was son of Numayn - Numayn of the Mountain, that is, not the less illustrious ones of that name - and he was son of Zais.

Now some people will tell you that Zais was born of out wedlock, but those are lies. He was the legitimate son of Ghutan, and Rasad 'Ban Ghutan' doesn't deserve that name, he should be called the 'Bastard,' not Zais. Anyway, as for Ghutan's father... Well, not everyone knows this, but...
I'm sorry. Are you not paying attention?
Oh.. Of course I am! This is fascinating. But tell me about your own deeds.
Do you have a trade? Any skills? Or just a string of ancestors?

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the athabaskan. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.

I am a warrior. I would recite to you my lineage, but that would take an hour. I would tell you my deeds, but that would take two. So, instead - if you pay me - I shall come with you and fight your enemies, and that will be the best demonstration of my mettle.
I will tell you. Perhaps you will think I am petty-minded, but a man's reputation is a valuable thing...

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the athabaskan. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

The great names in our great clans - some of them are brave, and generous with the loot, but don't they like to take their names bandied out after every battle? Poets know there's silver in it if they sing the praises of the Banu Qild, the Banu Sarran - but those of us who are Banu Nobody, well, we deserve a bit of time in the sun too, don't you think?
I fought three battles under the banner of the Sultan, and two more under the banners of the Qild. No more.
Indeed. Glory is as much a spoil of war as any, and should be shared.
Frankly, I have little time for glory-hounds of any sort. Men who do their job is what I want.
At any rate, I will find a master who allows me to win fame for myself. Or barring that, land and silver, so that I can buy a poet or two.

I am a warrior, but I am not from one of the greater clans. After a battle, I may get a bloodstained weapon pried from the enemy's hand or a pat on the head from my emir, but no song of my deeds. No robe of honor. I intend to fight for someone who see in people more than their name.
I will tell you my story. I haven't... I haven't spoken of this before, to anyone. Perhaps it's the wine here. But know that if you speak of this to anyone else, I'll cut your tongue out.

I have a gift... From the Heavens, perhaps, or perhaps from somewhere else. I have never met anyone I could not kill in a fair fight. But I do not like wars. Armies are full of crude men, boasters, drunks, rapists. I have another speciality.

Say you had a man you wanted killed. Who you would pay to kill. I could find him, bump into him, mutter an insult. He would pull out his blade. And that would be the last mistake he would ever make. But as I said, it would be a fair fight. I do not kill from behind. It is dishonorable.

But there was a lord, a customer of mine, who had no honor. And he refused to pay me. And having no honor, he laughed at my insults. He did not pull his blade. He had his men drive me away. I can kill one man but not three at once. So here I am.
You know, I'm sure you could put your gift to better use.
What you call 'honor'... I'm not sure that's the best word for it.
Mmm.... Well, for now, I do not know what to do with myself. Perhaps I could consider joining a warband, if the commander was well-bred and kept his word.

I am a sword for hire. Some think us scum but I have my own code of honor. If I kill a man, it must be in a fair fight. My last employer asked me to do something dishonorable, so now I am looking for a new employer.
Yeah, sure.

I come from a town where every alley has its 'protector.' These are men with some strength but also a lot of respect, who stand up for the rights of the people there. My father was our alley's protector, and so it fell on me to take his job after he grew too old to do it himself.

A few years after he retired, we had a new guard captain. We protectors, we serve the state, but we're not its tool. This new captain didn't understand. He'd come to me and say, 'One of my lads took this man's daughter - see that he doesn't make a fuss,' or, 'Let's have little private meetings, so you can tell us what your people are up to.'

I told the captain that I couldn't do these things. The alley people - they had to trust me. The captain didn't take 'no' for an answer. He pressured me. He threatened my father. What could I do? I couldn't betray my people but I couldn't betray my father either. I took my family and left.
A hard choice.
Better to have properly constituted authority than that of some back-alley tough.
So here I am. I have mouths to feed, and the thing I know best is to fight.

I'm from a town near here. I won't say which one... Our family were protectors of our alley, and by that I mean that I thumped the head of anyone who tried to take away our rights. But the guard captain, he kept coming around demanding money and favors, and I couldn't thump his head. So now I'm looking for new work.
You want a story? Then go toss a copper to a fellow who knows the song of Kais and Layali, because you won't get one from me.
Here's what you need to know about me - I can take a man down with a single blow, or maybe two if he's got armor, and I have expensive tastes in wine and women. So I don't work for free.
I kill for a living. Some men, in my line of work, will spin a tale of how they were forced into it, orphans of war or some-such. Piss on that.
I like to fight, I'm good at it, and in my opinion, the Heavens smile on a man who loves his job.
Can't fault you for enthusiasm, I suppose.
That's a rather unique theology.
You want me to kill for you? Then make me an offer. If not, piss off.
I kill for a living. If you want me to kill for you, pay me what I'm worth. If you don't, then don't waste my time.
Since you ask who I am, stranger, I will tell you.
The searing gravel plain knows me, as do the rippling sands and the shadowed canyon. The hidden spring whispers to me, 'Come hither and drink,' and the high outcrop unveils to me the horizons.
The viper does not trouble me, nor does the scorpion. I have faced the scouring sandstorm, the rushing flood, the killing heat of noontime, and they have all said to me, 'Pass safely, brother.'
I am {MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME}, prince of the wastelands, lord of solitude, master of emptiness. If you wish to know my other names, you may ask my kinsmen, the leopard, the hyena and the gazelle..
{MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME} is fine. No need to bother the hyenas. So, what can you do?
Master of empty talk, rather.

I roam the desert. I learn its secret ways, its gifts, as a lover learns the secrets and gifts of his beloved. But though the desert is bountiful, horses and steel must be bought with silver. So, I must sell my services from time to time.
I am of the desert. I know its ways. The wind guides me. The scorpion comes into my camp at night and tells me its secrets. The howls of the jackal bring me news of the hunt.
Hmf. Very well. I'll tell you - and you can decide for yourself whether my family should be ashamed of me.

I was part of a clan that lived beyond the mountains to the south. We came under pressure from our neighbors, who wanted to take our lush grazing grounds in the foothills. We were an ancient clan, that valued its name, but in this generation we have been short of men, so I fought alongside my brothers - indeed, I slew our enemies' champion in single combat. That stopped the pressure on our lands, but not the violence.
We kept our grazing grounds. But my brothers and cousins found that, when they mingled with other clans during the holy months of truce, that they were mocked. 'You let your women do your fighting!'

The insults were many, and they had no choice but to respond. One cousin was slain in a duel, one cousin killed his opponent, so we had two new bloodfeuds on our hands. I chose to leave home before it got any worse.
An impossible situation...
Honor must come first!
I find that I like to fight, and the pay is good. But I will do my fighting far from home, so that no shame attaches itself to my family's name.

I was a daughter of a wealthy clan. But our rivals drove us from our grazing grounds. We had to sell our herds. We were mocked in towns when we went to trade in the marketplace. Luckily my father was one of those wise enough to teach his daughters to fight. With the Heavens' help I will become wealthy and famous, and restore our family name.
I can tell you my story. If you spend time among merchants, I suppose you will hear it anyway, told as a cautionary tale, complete with a great deal of moralizing and tut-tutting.

My father was a merchant. When he died, he left his children a small inheritance. Most went to my brothers. They headed east, to the lands of the Padishah, leaving me in charge of our interests in Calradia. For me to step into my father's shoes, and be treated as an equal by other merchants, I knew I had to make a lot of money in a short time or they would elbow me out of the market.

I had an opportunity to buy pepper from another trader who was selling at a discount, and needed cash. I of course inspected the pepper and its storage. I interviewed the watchmen at the warehouse. You can trust us madame,' they said. 'Rest assured your pepper is in good hands.'

But one of them kept a brazier lit at night, for the warmth, and a camel kicked it into a bed of straw when he was off relieving himself. When he returned, the warehouse was in flames. And so became penniless.
Merchants take risks. I am sorry it turned out so badly for you.
All one's pepper in one warehouse. A cautionary tale indeed.

Well... Even now I feel I made a wise choice to buy the pepper -- wise, but unlucky. Such is fortune! Had I not seized this opportunity, other merchants would have mocked me, a woman who lacked the daring to succeed in a man's trade. Instead they mock a rash woman who lacked a man's judgment. And here I am, looking for work.
My parents were merchants, and I inherited a share of their workshops and camels. But banditry and the fortunes of trade ruined me, which is also common, and now I must make my money some other way.
Oh, I'll tell you my story. I don't mind who knows.

When I was a child, my mother sent me out on the streets to beg and pick pockets. And the big man of our quarter took a cut of that. I got a little older and my mother taught me how to rob drunken travellers, and the big man took a cut of that.

But you see, for a big man, it's not all sitting in the shade and counting your money. A big man must beat and he must kill, or people will not fear you. And one day, as I watched, he beat my mother to death over the share of his cut.

Now some would say I should have avenged my mother. But there was a wrinkle, you see - we didn't talk about it much, but he was my father, as he was the father of so many other children of our alley. So I fled our town, and now work here, using the skills my dear parents taught me.
Perhaps you can rise above the sorry circumstances of your birth.
They never cease to shock me, the sordid tales you hear from the dregs of the alleys.
So... Anyway, if you've got an enterprise or two that might not be entirely legal, and need a sharp eye on the villains you've got running it, you may find that my skills are of use to you.

I had no father, see. None that I knew. There are scores of us in every town, begging and stealing and working for the gangs. But I was always the type of girl who wanted something more, and I got ahold of this sword, you see, and now I intend to turn other people's blood into silver.
I'll tell you my story. I suppose it is a fine lesson in how destiny makes mock of our intentions.

My father was a judge, and I had intended to study the legal rulings of the past, so I could follow in his footsteps. But when I went to study, my master told me that only two kinds of scholars were needed these days: those who knew how to build and knock down walls, and those who knew how to stem the epidemics that spread from unburied bodies.

I had no talent for medicine, it turned out, so I chose to be an engineer. I had one final flight of folly - a local academy was crumbling, so I submitted a sketch for a new one to the emir. He laughed and told me to come back with a schematic of siege engines.

So go on - ask me how thick a mangonel's struts must be to withstand the torsion to throw a five-istar ball. Ask me how heavy a ram's head must be, compared to its total weight, so that it does not rebound from the gate and strike the men who wield it. I never imagined I would know such things, when I dreamed of making men's lives better through the dispensing of justice.
Well, some day there may be peace, and money to build again.
The quarries are hiring. You could always haul rocks for a living, if you're so averse to launching them.

Unfortunately, I've found that siegework pays irregularly. My contracts are usually honored if the city falls and is looted. But if dysentery breaks out in the siege camp and the army must march away, well, you may find that you submit your receipts in vain.

My father was a judge, and as such, I was educated to be a judge. That is usually the case with us. But I was always better at mathematics than letters. So I took mercenary work, making catapults. My father cast me out of his home in disgust. He once told me that the greatest privilege on earth is to dispense justice, but he will never know the joy of firing a mine and seeing the walls of a tyrannical baron or cruel archon crumble, so what does he know?
Certainly. The more who know about my skills, the better.

The women in our family passed down the art of healing from generation to generation, and other... em... services, that can be accomplished with herbs. But for all our skill we remained poor, while richly robed, well-fed men with half our skill walked about the towns tending to the lords and ladies.

By the time I became a woman I was sick of filthy huts and puking babies. I came to the towns and inquired after which households, among those who had wealth, might have a patient for me. Of course when I showed up at the door in my torn, stained dress they slammed it in my face.

So I acquired some denars - I will not say how - and with it bought a silk robe and some jewelry. This got me inside the doors of rich men's houses, and the cures I worked, and the reputation I earned, have done the rest.
Sounds like you have a good head for business.
Yes - many is the healer who has come to specialize in the diseases of the rich.

But I've noticed something - more denars is spent on war than on anything else. So, if someone's raised an army, and doesn't want to lose their investment to infected wounds and fevers, well, it might be worthwhile to employ me.
Once I was just another back-country healer, attending to squalling babies and superstitious villagers. But now I'm trying to make the money that my skill with medicine deserves.
Pull up a chair, friend - you'll be glad you asked!

I could tell you of all my deeds, and you'd never believe me. But you know, if you'd met me a year back, I could have taken you to my hall some time and shown you them. Shown you my deeds! You heard that!

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true Battanian never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

A lot of heads... You can imagine, a lot of other warriors were envious of me. Some in my village even conspired against me, had me expelled. I lost my hall, and I had to bury the heads. I doubt you could recognize them any more. What a pity, eh? A collection like that will never be seen again.
Envy, yes, the only possible explanation for why your clan drove you out. Such a terrible sin!
I doubt you have such a collection, and if you did, it would be the last thing I'd like to see.
So anyway, I need money to build a new hall, and start a new collection. So if someone wants to pay me my worth as a warrior, my spear is theirs!

Well now, I am a warrior of the Battanians. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.
I'll tell you. You may wish to get yourself a drink.

You may have heard of my father - Cynan fen Aedeg. Many called him Cynan the Brave. It's my life's goal to be his worthy son, though he died when I was a baby. My stepfather, though rich in land and cows, does not have the same reputation, although I resolved early in my life that duty to my mother necessitated that I serve him as loyally as I would my natural father.

Soon after I came of age, we got wind that our neighbors would raid us for cattle. We did not know by which road they would come. I was sent with a few of our tenants to hold a ford that was far out of the way.

At first I was angered, because I believed that I was being kept away from battle and glory. But as it turned out, that's the way the enemy army came. When I saw them at the ford, I challenged their leaders to single combat, as that was our way. They accepted, and sent forth a champion. To make a long story short, I slew him, and then two more who came after him. The rest graciously admitted that my victories meant they were obliged to retreat.
May all of us have such honorable foes!
A boy like you killed three champions, eh? Well, all things are possible, I suppose.

When I returned to my stepfather's hall, my mother met me outside, in tears. She had given me up for dead - my stepfather knew the direction from which the enemy clan would come, and had intended for me to die. She did nothing to stop him, but since I had survived, she bid me flee - for if not, she feared, it was inevitable that our clan should sink into the abyss of kinslaying. So here I am, looking for a worthy lord for whom to fight.

I was raised in a well-known clan, but my father died and my stepfather cast me out. It is a common enough story among our people. You may find many of us wandering the roads, our swords our only inheritance.
One moment. I need a drink.

I am Battanian. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most Battanians my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

But there's no legions any more. And since Caladog became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'Battania'? There is no Battania. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.

Every time I've fought with a band of my 'countrymen,' I've told them: 'Hold your lines. Stay firm. Fight as the Empires does: as a solid hammer, not a gaggle of goats.' And every time I have seen them disintegrate into a screaming rush as soon as the arrows start flying, to dash themselves on the enemy's shields or be cut down by cavalry coming in on the sides.
Indeed. There's much to be learned from the foreigner, whoever the foreigner is to you.
A man should fight for his hearth and his kin, however much they disappoint him.
Anyway, well, I've had it with narrow escapes from charging cataphracts, and I'm going to seek work in a more professional force.

I am Battanian by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?
I shall tell you. Is there a bard in the house? He may wish to take notes. I believe this is fine material for a song.
I am a connoisseur of horseflesh, my friend. No one knows horses better than I. But I find, alas, that often the best horses are wasted on unworthy owners, so I try to rectify that.

I was raised as a stableboy. But I had a gift for breaking horses, and for my hard work, and the risks I took to my neck taming young stallions, the old lord promised me that on my fifteenth birthday I should have a horse of my own.

But the old lord died, alas, and when my birthday came, his heir laughed at me. He told me that a fine horse would be wasted on me; perhaps I would like a goat. So that night I took the best animal in the stable, and rode off.
So, what you're saying is that you're a horsethief.
Of course. Every felon is just an honest man wronged. I've heard a hundred such tales and I've no wish to hear another.

I am the prince of horsethieves! I have stolen Aserai mares from amid the tents and ridden them across the desert under the moon, I have taken Vlandian stallions from their paddocks, the sturdy ponies of the Khuzaits, and the steady geldings of the imperial lancers. But, I'll be the first to admit, it is risky work, so sometimes I do other jobs.

I am a horsethief. I come from a region where to be a horsethief is an honorable profession, and I am very good at it. But it is dangerous work, as owners can be vindictive people, and I am seeking safer work - as a mercenary, perhaps.
Give me a minute. It has been a long time since I spoke more than a few words at a time to others.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the Battanians, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Wolfskins. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.
Some speak well of their time in the Wolfskins. It is intended to teach you the ways of the woods. But the 'pack' I joined were all rich feral children, playing at being animals.

They would sit around the fire at night and belittle each other. I was never quick with my tongue and the others learned to gang up on me. At one point I could take it no longer - I stabbed one in a fight. No one knew how to treat the wound, so he bled to death. And then I fled.
Good thing you were exempt from the laws of man, eh?
Barbarians. Just when you think you've heard it all... Good day to you.

I saw how much tradition was worth. I was not answerable to the law, but I heard soon enough that the family of the youth I'd stabbed hired men to kill me. I stayed in the woods, living alone. I am happy there, most of the time. But sometimes I yearn to be among other men, and come to the city to look for work.
I'm a former Wolfskin. No doubt you have heard of us. I am not proud of what I did as a Wolfskin. But I am proud of the woodcraft I learned.
Oh, I'll tell you. It's a fine tale, full of adventure and romance, but tragic too.

Aye, once I made a fine living, in the Empire, stopping merchants on the roads and asking 'em for a bit of change. But there was a lass there, beautiful as the moon and just as cold, and she was my undoing. Courted by an imperial prefect but I thought, I can do better than that, with my takings, and I brought her the pick of the rings and finery and asked her to pass the evening with me.

She agreed, eagerly enough! There was wine and talk, but too much wine, and I slept off. Then woke in the morning, I did, and hooves were clattering outside and up comes the prefect and a file of horsemen, and away they took me to the town to be hanged.

Blessed be the Gods, happened that my cousin Aed was in the guard. He sprung me that night from the prison, and together we went roaming round the country. But a passing magistrate decided he weren't parting with his purse, and pulled his blade rather than handing it over like a sensible lad. I took him down, but now before my poor Aed was butchered. See now the price of woman's ingratitude?
Most unlucky you were.
Perhaps one should not press a courtship too far, when one is a bandit.

So here I am now, drinking to my poor cousin's memory, and looking for a bit of honest work. Well, it needn't be too honest, I suppose. I have a few skills that might be of use - among other things, if you ever happen to acquire any contraband you wish to sell, I reckon I can spot you a good price in the markets.

I was a robber on the highways, in the Empire, making a fine living from the merchants on the roads. But I loved a girl in town, and snuck in to visit her from time to time. Then I got caught, and had to reveal the hiding place all my hard-earned loot to the guards to escape the noose. So here I am now.
Aye, I can tell you my story.

I was a cowherd. In most villages, this is a boy's job, because one must be alone in the hills. In our village there were few boys, and I was a good shot with a sling, good at keeping the wolves away.

The boys of the neighboring village would pester me. One of them, the chief's son, would not leave me alone. They wanted from me what all boys want. One day he came up behind me and tried to take me by force. But I had a knife...
I did not know what to do with his body. I buried it up in the hills, then told my parents. For fear of bloodshed, they told me to leave, to find my way in the world some other way.
It sounds as though you had no choice.
There are customs for that sort of thing, trials, blood money, you know.
I am no warrior, not yet - but I could be one. I am good with a sling, and a knife. I can run fast. I can bear hardship. I would stand my ground, because I have nowhere to run.

I was a shepherd. Normally the job is given to boys, but I always had a knack for bows and slings, which we use to keep the wolves away. The trouble with being a shepherd, though, is that there's always the chance of quarrels with the herders of the neighboring village over disputed pastures or missing sheep. Perhaps I was too good with a bow - I killed a neighbor. My parents were poor and could not afford the blood money, so I fled.
So, you want to know about the games that Fate has played with me?

When I was just a baby, a woman said to have the Sight came to my father's hall. When she saw me, she told him that she saw the mark of the faeries upon me. She performed a divination, and said she had learned that I was to be a prank played on mankind: I should grow up to be a great beauty, but that any man who proposes to marry me shall die.

Well, he did not believe in such things, so he laughed, tossed her a few coins, and sent her on her way. I grew up. When my first suitor was skewered by a spear in battle, I grieved, but thought little of it.
When my second suitor passed of a fever, I was unnerved. When my third suitor was thrown from his horse on a hunt, I knew I must do something..
Very responsible of you. Can't go killing off the whole village, now.
The trouble with prophecies... People remember the one that came true, never the ten that were false.

I resolved to take up the profession of arms, so that all men know that I am not the marrying type. I forge my own weapons, to avoid going into town whenever possible. And I tell all others of the curse upon me, as soon as I meet them. And I am far from my family, so no man will go to my father to ask for my hand.

I come from the highlands. My people were suspicious folk. It is easy to them to get into their heads that a child, especially a girl, practices witchcraft. I had two neighbors die of fevers within the same season, and so I was chased from my home and driven to fend for myself. Which I can, and did. I forge my own weapons and can wield them as well, but now I'm looking for steady work.
My story? This is my tale in a nutshell - men's greed for cattle cost me my home and my kin.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the Battanian upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.
We came down on the thief's village one day at dawn. They were too many, and we were beaten. My brothers and most of my kin were all slain. I had nowhere to go.

But I had killed three men with a spear that day, and found I had a taste for it. And I learned that thieves grow rich, while honest men die. So I lived in the hills, and took the cows of families more fortunate then my own. But I sold the cows I took, and kept the denars close to my chest.
Hard to blame you for that, I suppose.
When a victim turns thief, that does not right the world.
But I don't intend to live this way forever. There are a thousand paths to turning outlaw, you see, but they mostly come to a single end. So I'm here, in the town, looking for other work.

My family was in a feud. Over stolen cattle, as is often the case in the upcountry. Well, the family we fought turned out to be rather stronger than us, and most of us were killed. The rest were scattered. I lived for a while as a thief, stealing to eat, but that is a bitter path, and now I am looking for something better.

Hmm. Many men would begin their story by reciting their ancestry. I will not do this. A man should be judged on his own deeds, and a long list of ancestors does him no credit. Also, my family does not acknowledge me, so why should I acknowledge them?
I was the son of a household slave in a coastal kasbah, but my father bought my freedom when I was young and sent me to learn from a healer and a caravan-master.
I learned words of plants and of long routes across the High Plateaux; when trade wagons left for Sijilmasa or across to al-Andalus I would go with them and tend the men.
Medicine did not promise steady coin, so I took to travelling with caravans as a surgeon and guard. The desert makes a man patient — and sharp with a blade when he must be.
A hard-earned trade.
Service on caravans breeds more thieves than saints.
Now I wait for a caravan or an emir who pays fairly. I can stitch, bind, and guide; I can also show a caravan the secret springs of the desert.
Born low, trained to heal and guide caravans. I seek employers who value knowledge of the desert and hands that mend as well as strike.
I shall tell you... Ahem...
My father's name is known across a dozen valleys, my grandfather's as well — we have a lineage that some men recite with pride. I can recite our genealogy as others recite prayers.
These things matter when chiefs parley and bonds are sworn. But lineage alone does not feed a sword-arm or buy a good mount.
So I sell my blade where men will pay for skill, not only for a name. The desert listens to deeds more than to pedigrees.
A princely tone for a mercenary life.
If your lineage buys you nothing, I recommend a new one that pays.
I fight for those who count coin and oath alike. If you need a sworn man who remembers from whence he came, I'm for hire.
A man of proud blood who nevertheless takes service. If you pay honorably, you'll have a man who remembers to keep his word.
I will tell you. Perhaps you will think I am petty-minded, but a man's reputation is a valuable thing...
I belong to a lesser clan who answer to larger confederations when called; when banners were raised for the emir the great names took most of the glory.
We are not unknown for lack of courage, only for lack of poets. After a victory the songs speak of the great house while our axes go unmentioned.
So I left to find my own renown under a banner that might recognize me as more than a shadow of another. Perhaps a captain will grant a man a name worth singing.
Glory and its unequal distribution is an old complaint.
Better to have coin and land than a song that fades.
I'll find a master who sees the man as well as the clan. Or I'll find land and buy the poet myself.
A warrior of a lesser clan who seeks a banner that will let him rise from the ranks and earn his own song.
I will tell you my story. I haven't... I haven't spoken of this before, to anyone. Perhaps it's the wine here.
I have a gift for blades. A man I cross will step out and draw steel before he knows why he has done so.
I do not like courts and mustered hosts. A battlefield is ugly and chaotic; I prefer an artful stroke when the terms are mine.
But a lord who refuses to pay me once laughed and turned me out. I can take one man fairly; I can't stand ten at once. So here I am, looking for work with captains who keep their word.
A dangerous man with a code.
Honor is a convenient excuse for murder.
For now I’ll join a captain who keeps faith. I fight fair, but I fight hard.
A sword for hire with a strict code: all fights must be fair. One who values courtesy in the cutting of throats.
Yeah, sure.
I grew up where every bazaar lane had its protector — men who kept watch over trade and exacted a cut. My father was one of them, and I learned how to keep order in narrow alleys.
When a new governor's captain came and demanded bribes and 'cooperation', my father refused. He was beaten and our house was marked.
We left rather than bend the knee. I now make my living in far towns where no one knows my surname and I can sell my arm as needed.
A hard choice indeed.
Better to serve a lawful captain than a corrupt official.
I will guard caravans or a market for honest coin. My loyalty goes where it is earned.
An alley-warden who will not bend to corruption. If you need a watch on goods or a steady hand in a fight, I'm for hire.
You want a story? Then toss a coin — stories are expensive.
I'm a blade's man. I take coin, no piety; nobles spin tales of being forced into violence. Piss on that.
If a man stands against me and will not yield, I end it quickly. I prefer good wine and the comfort of a warm tent.
Ask if I will work for you, and I will answer plainly: name your price and I will tell you whether I will accept it.
No argument there.
You have an interesting philosophy.
If you need a killing done, do not ask for sentiment. Ask for coin and discretion.
I kill for coin and pleasure. Pay well and have no regrets.
Since you ask who I am, stranger, I will tell you.
The searing plains and the high gorges know me. I have guided flocks, led raids across the passes, and brought caravans safely through sand and bandit.
The viper and scorpion pass me by; no storm has broken my camp. The desert teaches its favourites to read wind and hoof like men read speech.
I am {MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME}, and I answer to names of beasts and stars alike. If you need a guide, I know the hidden wells and the tracks the caravans use in dark months.
{MET_WANDERER.FIRSTNAME} is enough. Will you guide a caravan?
Master of empty words, are you?
I roam the desert and sell my knowledge. Horses cost coin even to the Bedouin; I must sometimes take service to keep my mounts.
A desert-scout and caravan-master; I know springs and ambushes and will bring your wagons through if you pay fairly.
Hmf. Very well. I'll tell you - and you can decide whether my family should be ashamed of me.
We were a clan in the green foothills until raiders and rival chiefs took our grazing; we fought and managed to keep our herds by single combat, but it left kinless and weary men behind.
When clansmen mocked that our women fought for us, old grudges flared. Bloodfeuds took our young men until the household could not recover.
I left to find my own fortune — fight for wage, not for the shame or pride of others, and one day buy land to restore our name.
A hard path but an honourable one.
Honor first, money second, as always.
I fight far from home so the taunts won't follow my family. If I can earn enough to buy pasture, I will return and be honoured as I desire.
A daughter of dispossessed stock who learned arms; she fights to restore family standing with coin and deed.
I can tell you my story, as merchants love to trade in tales of ruin and recovery.
My father was a merchant and left me a share of caravans and wares. When he died, my brothers went east; I stayed to mind the goods.
I bought a load of pepper at a discount, trusting the warehouse and its watchmen, only to have a brazier knocked over by a camel or servant in the night.
The store went up and so did my capital. Now merchants laugh at me as a rash woman who trusted poorly. I left that trade and took to wandering.
A merchant's risk, misfortune was yours.
All of one's spice in one store — a harsh lesson.
Fortune goes to the brave and the lucky. I wager again now, in men and in opportunity rather than warehouses.
A merchant's daughter ruined by fire who now sells her sword or services; trade taught me to judge men fast.
Oh, I'll tell you my story. I don't mind who knows.
As a child my mother sent me to the souk to beg and pick pockets; the big man of our quarter took a cut, as is the way of those who rule the back-alleys.
One day he beat my mother to death over a share. The truth is messy — that man was also my father; the sort of thing such streets breed.
I fled then, and made a living with the skills my parents taught me. Now I prefer blades to begging.
You can rise above the mean beginning.
Those are dire tales from the alleys indeed.
If you have ventures of dubious legality needing a discreet and sharp watcher, I may be of service.
An alley orphan who learned to steal and to fight; now I use those skills on the road for coin.
I'll tell you my story. A fine lesson in fate, if nothing else.
My father was a qadi; I'd been tutored to study law and scripture, to be learned and measured.
But when my teacher told me the world wants practical men — those who know siege engines and how to stop pestilence — I discovered my head fit numbers and geometry better than words.
So I became an engineer of sorts, making contrivances for sieges and for irrigation, though learned men scorned me for leaving the madrasa.
A scholar of action rather than words.
Ha — the quarries want hands more than verses.
Siege-work pays when the city falls. When it does not, receipts are but paper. I take what coin I can find and keep moving.
Trained in geometry and siegecraft, I am an engineer who prefers earth and rope to ink. Seek me if you need walls taken or mended.
Aye, I can tell you of my craft, if you’ve a moment and a flagon to share.

I was born in Ulm, apprenticed to a guild mason who served both abbots and dukes. We built churches that kissed Heaven and bridges that defied the Rhine’s fury. I learned that stone listens only to patience, not pride.

When the Emperor quarreled with Rome, our monastery patrons lost their coin. The masons scattered, some to Italy, some to ruin. I took my compass and chisel and walked where work still called for them.
Now I sell my hands to whoever builds strongholds or tears them down. Stone is honest—men, less so.
You sound a craftsman with both pride and sense. I’ll remember that.
A man who serves both abbots and dukes must know how to survive between hammer and anvil.
Hire me, and I’ll raise your towers square and true—or pull your enemy’s down to dust.
A Swabian mason-engineer, versed in cathedral and castle alike. Once loyal to abbots, now loyal to silver.
God’s grace, you wish my story? Few men care for the tale of a servant knight.
My family were ministeriales, unfree knights sworn to a bishop in Mainz. We held land at his pleasure, rode at his command, and bled at his wars. I dreamed of honor, yet found only obedience.
When the bishop backed the Pope, the Emperor seized his estates. We were cast adrift—lords without title, soldiers without pay. I learned that chivalry tastes bitter when seasoned with hunger.
Now I sell my sword to any banner that flies high and pays honest coin. God forgive me, but loyalty alone feeds no man.
A knight by duty, not birth. That earns respect more than gold ever will.
I’ll not fault a man for surviving his lord’s ruin.
If you’ve need of a steady lance and sober counsel, I can serve. I’ve ridden with priests and princes alike, and I know the weight of both.
A dispossessed ministerialis knight of Mainz, loyal once to Church and now to whoever keeps faith with silver.
By Saint Ulrich, I’ve fought for every fool who could afford a banner.
I began as a footman under Count Welf’s levy, slogging through mud and fire in Italy. When the paymaster forgot our wages, I took command of those who’d still follow me—and found I’d a gift for it.
We sold our strength to city leagues and quarrelsome dukes alike. Once I kept order in Augsburg for three months, till the burghers realized they’d hired wolves to guard their sheep.
Now I ride alone. The men I led lie buried from Lombardy to the Elbe, and my sword still hungers. War is my trade, but death’s the only sure wage.
A captain without a company is a fire without wood—eager to catch again.
You’ve seen too many campaigns to need sermons from me.
If you seek order among rabble, I’ll forge it. I ask no titles—only coin, discipline, and a cause worth dying for.
A battle-scarred mercenary captain of Bavarian stock, once commander of a Free Company. Cunning, loyal, and utterly without illusion.
You’d not guess by my robes, but I once stood beside princes at council.
I studied letters in Würzburg and law in Bologna, copying charters till my eyes burned. For a time I served as notary to an archbishop, drafting decrees that bound lords tighter than chains.
When the Investiture quarrel tore Empire from Church, my ink turned from scripture to accusation. One day I wrote the writ that condemned my own mentor. I left that night and never returned.
Now I lend my quill to merchants and warlords. A sharp mind buys freedom, if one’s conscience can afford the cost.
Knowledge is a blade few wield safely. You seem to manage it.
A learned man in rough company—let’s hope your wit cuts faster than a sword.
If you need letters written, laws twisted, or treaties sealed, I’m your man. I swear my ink flows true, even when the truth bends.
A wandering clerk and scholar from Würzburg, once in service to bishops. Quick with quill and conscience alike.
Ja, I’ve been called brigand, thief, and worse. But hunger has no saints.
I was born to peasants near Erfurt. When famine came, I took to the woods with others like me. We robbed grain carts bound for the abbey and fed the starving. For that, they named us bandits.
I saw good men hang while fat monks prayed for their souls. I swore never again to kneel before a lord who’d sell salvation for coin.
Now I know the backroads, the tollkeepers, and which sheriffs take bribes. Call me outlaw if you must—but remember, outlaws still know honor.
A man who steals for bread may yet fight for justice.
Keep your hands where I can see them, friend.
If you need safe passage or quiet work done under moonlight, I can manage it. I’ve made peace with the law—by staying two steps ahead of it.
A Thuringian outlaw turned guide and scout, shrewd and loyal once trust is earned.
You’ll find few who wish to hear a surgeon’s tale over supper.
I learned medicine in the infirmary at Regensburg, stitching pilgrims and monks alike. Blood teaches faster than books—if you live long enough to learn.
When plague struck, I bled men by the dozen and prayed thrice as often. Some lived, most did not. The abbey blamed my hands, not God’s will, and cast me out.
Since then I’ve tended soldiers in the field, nobles in secret, and thieves in alleyways. All men are equal when their breath rattles.
Mercy takes many forms. Yours simply stains the hands.
If you can keep my men standing, I’ll not ask which saints approve.
I’ll serve your company faithfully. I charge by the wound, not the soul.
A Regensburg-trained surgeon, cast from holy service yet still sworn to heal. Stoic, weary, and indispensable.
Well, before we begin, here's a flagon of ale to your health - both physical and spiritual.
I fancy myself a healer, you see. My parents sent me to a Mercian monastery when I was young to study both prayers and herbs.
But the monasteries... lovely gardens, rich libraries, yet the dawn prayers and endless copying of texts felt hollow. I left to see the world.
I joined armies as a healer, tending to wounds both of flesh and spirit. I found I did more good on the road than among monks.
Yes, yes. The healer must go to where there is need of healing.
The monastic calling is supposed to inspire us to live pure lives. It doesn't look good when people abandon it.
I look for campaigns where I might serve and gain experience, learning more of both herbs and men.
I was a monk, but ill-suited to monastery life. I learned herbs and healing, and now wander, offering my skills to armies and lords alike.
Of course - and I'm sure you'll agree it's a tale worth telling!
I was born in Normandy, trained as a squire for Duke Robert. When the Conqueror’s sons called for men in England, I came to serve.
I saw castles and villages, and the cost of loyalty. I fought in skirmishes, learned quickly the harsh lessons of war.
Now I roam, seeking a lord who respects skill and courage, one who rewards action rather than birth.
A squire learning the ways of war in a foreign land.
The road from squire to knight is hard and full of tests.
I offer my sword to any lord in need, hoping to earn my spurs and honor in England.
I am a Norman squire in England. Trained in arms, I wander seeking opportunity to prove myself and earn my knighthood.
I can tell you my story, but I don't know how interesting you will find it.
I was born out of wedlock. My father raised me, but I had no inheritance. I took up the sword to make my own way.
I joined my village’s levy to defend against Norman tax collectors. None wished to fight, so I volunteered, earning my first taste of battle.
At a ford, I stayed behind while the rest fled, facing an enemy cavalry force alone. I survived, but it changed me forever.
I commend your love for your fellow man.
Mmm... I do appreciate virtue, but villainy makes for a much spicier tale.
I wander now, offering my blade to lords or causes that need a man who fears neither danger nor duty.
I am an Anglo-Saxon outlaw, born out of wedlock. I fight to survive and seek a new path where I can earn my place.
I'm drunk, so I'll tell you.
I fought in Normandy, then England, under William and his sons. I have seen sieges and battles that younger men would not survive.
Lords often send men to die for coin or land. I tire of serving such masters. My sword is mine to offer, not theirs.
I wander now, offering service to causes that respect honor, or to lords who value men as more than tools.
A veteran who knows both glory and folly.
Skill without a cause can be wasted. You seek rightly.
I take work with lords who respect knights, or with men who fight for survival. That is all.
I am a Norman veteran knight. I fought in Normandy and England, and now wander in search of honor and purpose.
A short tale, friend, but it bites sharp.
I was a fisherman along the Wash. Life was simple until a Norman sheriff seized my boat for taxes I could not pay.
I gathered men like me and raided ships and outposts, but never harmed innocents. We lived as outlaws.
Eventually, I tired of hiding. I wandered inland, offering my strength for coin or cause, always keeping my freedom above all else.
A rogue with principles. Unusual these days.
Many would call you a thief, yet you have your honor.
I now wander, taking work as a scout, mercenary, or guard. I am loyal to those who respect my code.
I am an Anglo-Saxon fisherman turned rogue. Forced to take up arms after injustices, I wander, offering my skill to those who respect the old ways or pay well.
A bow speaks louder than a tongue.
Born in Bayeux, I trained as an archer, skilled at long and short range, both horse and foot.
I came to England with Norman lords, fought at Hastings, and learned the price of arrows and men alike.
Now I wander, offering my bow to lords, mercenaries, or causes that respect skill over birth.
A fine marksman indeed.
Skill counts for more than name sometimes.
I take commissions where arrows are valued, and the dead are counted by honor, not coin.
I am a Norman archer, trained in Bayeux, veteran of Hastings, and now a wanderer offering skill to those who respect it.
I once served a king, now I serve only chance and coin.
I was the son of a thegn in Mercia, trained in arms and horse. Our lands fell to Norman lords, and I had to flee.
I fought alongside other dispossessed thegns to defend villages, and learned the art of ambush and raid.
Now I wander, offering my sword to any lord who respects a warrior’s skill.
A displaced thegn, noble by birth, skilled by experience.
The world takes and gives back little, but skill counts always.
I lend my sword to causes that pay in honor or protection, and travel freely otherwise.
I am an Anglo-Saxon thegn, dispossessed, wandering in England, offering my sword to those who value skill and courage.
My tale is of courts and castles, though not without peril.
I was a lady-in-waiting in the court of Queen Matilda, skilled in etiquette, embroidery, and listening where words are dangerous.
But I tired of hushed chambers and schemes. I wanted freedom, not a cage gilded in silk.
So I left, taking what I knew — courtly wit, some swordplay taught by my brothers — and wandered into the wider world.
A bold choice for a woman of court.
Freedom is worth more than comfort.
I now travel, lending counsel and subtlety where brute force alone would fail.
I was once a Norman lady-in-waiting. Now I wander, trading courtly knowledge for freedom.
A bow kept meat in my pot and raiders from my door.
I grew up in the Weald, where forest law pressed hard on us. The Normans claimed the king’s deer, but hunger knows no laws.
I poached, tracked, and laid traps. I knew every deer path and outlaw’s hideout between Sussex and Kent.
Soon I found it was not only game I could hunt — men too leave trails, and men too can be brought down by arrow or snare.
A hunter’s eyes are sharper than any sword.
Forest laws are cruel things. You turned hunger into skill.
Now I serve as scout or tracker, wherever men need prey found — beast or human.
I am an Anglo-Saxon hunter, trained by hunger and hardship, skilled in bow and track alike.
I sought glory — and still I do.
Born to a minor Norman lord, I had training but no inheritance. Tournaments and border wars became my stage.
I fought duels, won some, lost more. But I learned chivalry, and I learned the taste of dust.
Still, I wander. Each battlefield is a chance to prove worth, each victory a step toward glory.
Glory is a heavy burden, but a worthy goal.
Some seek gold, some seek God — you seek renown.
I offer my sword in service, for chance of honor, for hope of name.
I am a Norman knight errant, son of a minor lord, wandering for glory, tournaments, and cause.
A song is a blade of its own, you know.
I was born in Wessex, son of a reeve. My father wished me to till fields. I wished to sing of heroes.
I wandered with harp in hand, trading songs for food, hearing tales of Hastings, Ely, and rebellions.
I learned that words can raise courage or rebellion as sure as steel.
Coin buys loyalty, but steel keeps it.
I was born in Rouen, trained under men-at-arms who served William’s sons. Discipline was my life.
I fought in sieges, in rebellions, in border wars in Wales. Always with contract, always with pay.
But when lords default on their coin, captains must seek new service. That is the way of mercenaries.
A seasoned captain, then.
Coin may be your goal, but skill is your worth.
I now wander, commanding small bands or serving as captain-for-hire.
My tale is not soft, but it is mine.
I was a wife of a thegn, until Norman swords made me widow. They thought me helpless.
Your strength is hard-won and well-earned.
A woman forged by grief into steel.
I don't mind talking about it.
I am an engineer, trained in fortifications and siegecraft under the old imperial army. When the legions fell apart, many of my colleagues went into the lords' employ. I stayed true to my craft.
Nepotism runs rampant among engineers these days. Brothers and old apprentices get contracts while competent hands like mine are overlooked.
I refuse to cut corners. If a wall will crumble, I will say so. That honesty has kept me from the easier work, but I sleep soundly.
So I roam from town to town, taking work where I can find it—supervising construction, dismantling faulty defenses, or aiding in siege craft.
Most noble of you, sir.
A man of integrity, or simply one who backbites his peers? I have no idea, and wouldn't want to take the risk of hiring you.
I am an engineer trained in the imperial army. I travel for work, supervising construction, destruction, and siegecraft wherever needed.
You want to know about me? Well, that's a story, that's a story.
I have fought across Italy and beyond. My enemies have many names for me; some call me brave, others reckless. I answer only to myself.
Every fight I entered, I respected the rules. If you were my enemy, I gave you your chance, but never the innocent.
War is no game. Streets are no arena. If someone crosses you, act decisively. That is all one can trust in this life.
Merchants hire me as muscle or guard, but I owe allegiance to no one. I am a soldier of fortune, nothing more, nothing less.
Ah, yes. Wise words. Do go on.
You've said nothing about yourself, and your one word contradicts the other. I have better things to do.
I am a soldier of fortune. I fight for coin, skill, and survival—not for any lord or crown.
It is not without some reluctance that I tell this story, for it hardly does honor to my name.
My father was a cataphract in the east. We owned a modest estate to support his horse and armor. I was raised to follow in his path.
But the Cumans overran our land, and he was slain. I could not take up his horse and armor, so I turned to merchants, offering my skill for hire.
I work as a hired sword for merchants, yet I hope one day to reclaim the land I need to serve properly as my father did.
I try to choose my masters wisely, hoping that some honor from my equestrian training rubs off even in the courts of commerce.
That's it? The dishonorable part? That you work for merchants? I'd thought it would be a lot worse.
A cavalier of the Italian doing errands for traders! The shame of it!
I am a former imperial cataphract, now a mercenary for merchants, maintaining the skills and honor of my father where I can.
Refill my glass and I'll tell you.
I am a soldier by trade. I served in the Italian legions for twenty years, until betrayal and misfortune fractured our forces.
Many comrades died when Drosios Neretzes led an ambush against us. I was laid up sick. The army was never the same afterward.
The legions fell into the hands of the wealthy, who maintained soldiers at their own expense. Squabbling factions replaced discipline, and we were mocked by former enemies.
I now sell my sword to worthy commanders, training footmen and handling siege equipment for those who will follow skill over money.
No doubt a sad state of affairs. So what do you do?
Ah, the old days. And no doubt back then they complained about the older days. I've heard enough.
I am a soldier of the imperial legions, now a wandering instructor and mercenary, turning youths into disciplined fighters.
Oh, I suppose I can tell you. Nothing that no one doesn't already know, no how.
I ran away from my village to join men who made their living on the roads. Life plowing fields seemed too harsh for me.
Bandits are brutal animals—drunken, stabbing, dying of plague or hanging. I quickly learned the risks of that life.
I left that life, paid some friends to remove my name from the outlaw list, and became a law-abiding citizen, though I still enjoy the thrill of a fight.
Life in the city suits me better. The work can be rough, but I can relax afterward with better company than the forests offered.
A wise decision.
A knave who could not abide other men's knavery! May such wonders never cease.
I dabbled in crime as a youth, then struck out on my own. I am honest now, though I enjoy a fight when necessary.
You're a nosy one, I see.
My family? I care little for them. I left as a child and never regretted it. My brothers can keep their inheritance.
I fought in many wars. Comrades turn on each other in the end, and I prefer to keep my distance.
My past is mine alone. I speak little of it.
I fight for a living. I will take work others shy from, and I am skilled enough to handle it.
So... What are you good at?
You're a cheerful one. Good day to you.
I kill for a living. I take the work others will not, and I do it well.
I'll tell you my story.
I once followed Ladimos the Red, who preached rebellion against merchants and landowners. Many of us believed, others followed for debt or mischief.
We built a backcountry temple called the Kingdom of Truth, and fought imperial detachments. When Ladimos died, our group broke apart. Some turned to extortion to survive.
I left, and the emperor sent troops to finish the Kingdom of Truth. Former comrades now serve lords or languish in cages marked R for robber.
I learned skills for survival in the hills and on caravan routes. Now I seek honest work where I can use them.
A sad tale.
Heresy, rebellion, and looting are three intertwined serpents. You should bear that brand yourself, knave.
Once a rebel in the hills, I now seek honest work, skilled in survival and tracking.
Yeah, I'll tell you my story. Pass the wine and listen close.
My family owed debts, so I enlisted disguised as a man under a local commander. I preferred action to domestic life.
Dressing as a man was simple. I bound my chest and observed the duties without difficulty.
An ambush led to a rout. I survived, but the army life ended for me. Glory hounds led me to near death.
Merchants now give me work. I can wield, repair, or craft weapons and seek a captain with a company to join.
Well, there's always work for the brave and the resourceful.
A rather sad tale of deceit and disgrace.
I disguised myself to serve in the legions. Many have done the same, and survived to tell it.
I'll tell you my story. If it bothers you, I'd prefer you keep it to yourself - unless you've lived months on crusts of bread and chaff of grain, that is.
My father was a grain merchant in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. We lived comfortably until riots destroyed our home.
The guards burned our neighborhood. My father tried to save his strongbox but was killed. We joined refugees, living by our wits in the countryside.
I took a sword from a drunken guardsman. It has been invaluable since.
I adapt quickly. I could serve a warlord if given the chance, learning whatever skills are needed.
The starving do what they must.
And to think you had all the advantages of an educated childhood.
I am a merchant's daughter displaced by riots. Survival taught me skills that now keep me wandering yet capable.
Aye, so you want my story then?
As a child, I ran with a gang called the Centaurs in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}, running errands from pickpocketing to knife work.
I grew older and escaped the harassment of drunken men. Unsure where to go, I sought freedom.
My skills at stealth and knives became useful to merchants and minor lords. They pay well if you can handle discretion.
I now wander Italy, taking contracts that suit my talents, always avoiding the city watch.
You have talents, I see.
Talented, but dishonorable. I shall stay away from you.
I am a streetwise wanderer skilled in stealth, knives, and evasion, offering my talents to those who can pay.
I have studied much, though perhaps not enough.
Born to a minor noble family, I had access to scrolls, teachers, and rare texts in Latin, Greek, and Arabic.
I found the libraries of Pisa and Florence more interesting than court life. Studies became my rebellion.
The death of my patron forced me to wander. I teach, translate, and record histories as I go.
I look for scholars, merchants, and lords who value knowledge. Coins for study, or for teaching the young.
Ah, the life of letters. Admirable.
All that study and what does it bring? Only hunger and wandering.
I am a wandering scholar, translator, and teacher, seeking knowledge and employment wherever I go.
Careful now, some things are best left untold.
I trained in alchemy in Venice, studying herbs, metals, and the secrets of fire.
I discovered the limits of my teachers and set out on my own, concocting remedies, poisons, and oddities.
Some call me a charlatan, some a genius. I care little, so long as the work excites me.
Now I wander to find ingredients, clients, and patrons willing to fund experiments.
A curious life.
Dangerous, and foolhardy. I would keep my distance.
I am an alchemist wandering Italy, studying herbs, metals, and mysteries, serving patrons and experimenting wherever I can.
Then came the day that {IMPERIALCAPITAL} burned, and everyone was out looting and robbing, and that was my chance. Lifted a bag of silver from the Centaurs' stash and lit out on the road.
A hard life, but I must admire your fortitude, at least.
You truly are the dregs of the street, my lady.
Anyway, I wandered about a bit, but now I think it's time I found steady work. You wouldn't need someone to stick a knife in those that need sticking, do you?

I was an orphan, you see. Worked for a gang, as our kind must so often do. Did their foul work for them. But they perished in a siege, and I decided to strike out on my own, see what this fine land of Calradia could offer me.
I can tell you my story, though it is painful to recall.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Portuguese.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Portuguese, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

One time they came at midnight - they had a man who plotted against the Emperor, they said, and they needed a confession, and wished me to use my art to elicit that confession. If I refused, they said, they would disclose our relationship to my patients - I would be ruined. I went with them, to my shame, and what I was asked to do to that man's body -- I shall not repeat it.
You too are a victim of the hideous power of the state.
You broke your oath. It is not surprising that you fell further.

I should have refused - my practice was ruined anyway. To blot out the memory of that night, I took opium, until my pallid face so alarmed my patients that they no longer called on me. So I fled the city, and have wandered from town to town ever since. I would welcome steady work, if I could find it.

I was a surgeon, trained at the imperial academy. But my home and infirmary were burned in a bout of unrest, and now I must wander the world a bit. There are many of us out there, you know, forced to make what living we can.
Yes... I can tell you my tale...

My father was an imperial cataphract. Alas, he died in battle against the Arabs, and I was placed under the local archon's guardianship. He had eyes for my father's estate, modest as it was, so he arranged for me to be married to his cousin.

But this cousin... I would not marry that man! He was a boor, a drunk - never there was a night that he did not reek of wine, never a morning that he did not reek of vomit! But a cataphract's daughter is not some chit you can marry against her will. I took a horse from my father's estate - my horse, legally - his old sword, and rode off.

So, here I am. Perhaps I am not the most experienced of warriors, but I can learn. I cannot go back - I learned that the archon filed suit that I stole a horse - my own horse, by right! - which shows you what a cad he is.
You've got spirit, I'll give you that.
Takes more to being a warrior than a horse and a sword, young one.
